title: Authentication
description: In this guide, we'll look at how authentication works. NoMercy offers two ways to authenticate your API requests: Basic authentication and OAuth2 with a token.
content: authentication you'll need to authenticate your requests to access any of the endpoints in the nomercy api. in this guide, we'll look at how authentication works. nomercy offers two ways to authenticate your api requests: basic authentication and oauth2 with a token — oauth2 is the recommended way. classname: 'lead' basic authentication with basic authentication, you use your username and password to authenticate your http requests. unless you have a very good reason, you probably shouldn't use basic auth. here's how to authenticate using curl: please don't commit your nomercy password to github! oauth2 with bearer token the recommended way to authenticate with the nomercy api is by using oauth2. when establishing a connection using oauth2, you will need your access token — you will find it in the nomercy dashboard under api settings. here's how to add the token to the request header using curl: always keep your token safe and reset it if you suspect it has been compromised. using an sdk if you use one of our official sdks, you won't have to worry about any of the above — fetch your access token from the nomercy dashboard under api settings, and the client library will take care of the rest. all the client libraries use oauth2 behind the scenes. ::button url: '/sdks', variant: 'text' check out our list of first-party sdks ::icon arrow-right ::

title: Pagination
description: In this guide, we will look at how to work with paginated responses when querying the NoMercy API
content: pagination in this guide, we will look at how to work with paginated responses when querying the nomercy api. by default, all responses limit results to ten. however, you can go as high as 100 by adding a parameter to your requests. if you are using one of the official nomercy api client libraries, you don't need to worry about pagination, as it's all being taken care of behind the scenes. classname: 'lead' when an api response returns a list of objects, no matter the amount, pagination is supported. in paginated responses, objects are nested in a attribute and have a attribute that indicates whether you have reached the end of the last page. you can use the and query parameters to browse pages. example using cursors ::row ::col in this example, we request the page that starts after the conversation with id . as a result, we get a list of three conversations and can tell by the attribute that we have reached the end of the resultset. ::properties ::property name: 'startingafter', type: 'string' the last id on the page you're currently on when you want to fetch the next page. ::property name: 'endingbefore', type: 'string' the first id on the page you're currently on when you want to fetch the previous page. ::property name: 'limit', type: 'integer' limit the number of items returned. :: ::col ::

title: Errors
description: In this guide, we will talk about what happens when something goes wrong while you work with the API.
content: errors in this guide, we will talk about what happens when something goes wrong while you work with the api. mistakes happen, and mostly they will be yours, not ours. let's look at some status codes and error types you might encounter. classname: 'lead' you can tell if your request was successful by checking the status code when receiving an api response. if a response comes back unsuccessful, you can use the error type and error message to figure out what has gone wrong and do some rudimentary debugging before contacting support. ::callout every error response carries a type and a message that name what went wrong. read those first, since most errors are answered there. if the message does not explain it, that is worth reporting: an unclear error is a bug in the api, not in your code. :: error types ::row ::col whenever a request is unsuccessful, the nomercy api will return an error response with an error type and message. you can use this information to understand better what has gone wrong and how to fix it. most of the error messages are pretty helpful and actionable. here is a list of the two error types supported by the nomercy api — use these to understand what you have done wrong. ::properties ::property name: 'apierror' this means that we made an error, which is highly speculative and unlikely. ::property name: 'invalidrequest' this means that you made an error, which is much more likely. :: ::col ::

title: Common App Issues
description: Playback failures, login problems, and sync issues.
content: common app issues web app can't reach my server on my home network if you open the web app on the same network as your server and it never connects, your browser is almost certainly blocking the request as a security precaution. this is not a server misconfiguration, and there's nothing to fix on the server. symptoms - playback never starts, and live features the dashboard, live sessions, casting never connect. - the browser console repeatedly logs something like: - in firefox, a "local network access detected" permission banner appears until you allow it. why this happens app.nomercy.tv is served over the public internet. when you open it from a device on the same network as your server, dns resolves your server's hostname something like straight to its private lan address . modern browsers treat any request from a public site into a private or local-network address as sensitive and hold it back until you grant permission. chrome and edge call this private network access; firefox calls it local network access. it applies to every public site reaching into your lan, not just nomercy. your server already does its part: it sends on the cors preflight and serves a valid public tls certificate. the piece that's missing is the one-time permission your browser wants from you, not a fix on the server side. this only comes up when you're on the same network as your server. from outside your home network your traffic goes through the server's public tunnel instead of its lan address, so there's no private-network prompt and nothing to allow. fix firefox version 149 and later, rolling out to everyone from firefox 151: accept the local network access prompt when it appears. if you dismissed it, go to settings → privacy & security → permissions → local network access and allow . chrome / edge: allow local network access when prompted. if you missed the prompt, open the site settings for and enable local network access sometimes labeled insecure private network. skip it entirely: the nomercy android app and the infiniframe desktop app don't go through a browser, so this prompt never applies to them. opening the web app from outside your home network avoids it too, since that traffic never touches your server's lan address. firefox reconnects to the server in a rapid loop if the web app reaches your server but then firefox hammers it with a fast loop of failed connections the console fills with repeated errors that end in , that was a server-side problem with how the live connections rode over http/2. firefox is the only browser that carries websockets over http/2, so it was the only one that looped; chrome, edge, the android app, and the infiniframe desktop app were never affected. fix this is fixed on the server. update your nomercy media server to the latest version and the loop stops on its own, with no browser setting to change. if you can't update right away, the loop also stops if you set to in firefox's , but updating the server is the real fix and you can turn that back on afterward.

title: MediaServer Overview

title: Blocking Abusive Traffic
description: How the server detects vulnerability scanners, bans them automatically, and publishes a deny-list your firewall can consume.
content: blocking abusive traffic any server reachable from the internet gets scanned. within minutes of a new hostname appearing in the public certificate transparency logs, automated tools start asking it for wordpress admin pages, files and php shells. none of that exists on a nomercy server, so every one of those requests is someone checking whether you are worth attacking. the server watches for that pattern and bans the address it comes from. offences accumulate inside a rolling window, crossing the threshold produces a ban, and the ban expires on its own. if the same address comes back later, the next ban lasts longer. this is the same shape as fail2ban, running inside the server rather than beside it, which means it works whether you are reachable through a cloudflare tunnel or through a port forward on your router. what counts as an offence two things are treated as evidence. the first is a request for a path that belongs to software this server does not run. a request ending in , or containing , , , or , is scored heavily. no nomercy client, on any platform, ever asks for those. the second is a request for a path that never matched anything, from a caller who is not signed in. that is scored lightly, because a single one of those means very little on its own. two things are deliberately not offences, because getting either wrong would lock out real people: - a rejected request that did match a real endpoint. a client holding an expired token hammers the api with failures, and none of them count. your users cannot ban themselves by leaving a tab open over the weekend. - a missing static file. browsers ask for stale bundles and old icons after every deploy, and those misses are ignored entirely. addresses on your own network are never scored at all. that covers loopback, the private ranges , , , carrier-grade nat and ipv6 link-local and unique-local addresses. settings everything is in the dashboard under settings > security. there is nothing to put in a config file and no environment variable to set. | setting | default | what it does | |:--|:--|:--| | enabled | on | turns detection and enforcement off entirely when unchecked | | offence threshold | | score that triggers a ban. a known exploit path scores , an anonymous request that matched no route scores | | window | minutes | how long an offence stays on the tally | | ban length | minutes | length of a first ban. each repeat doubles it | | longest ban | days | ceiling the doubling never passes | | allowlist | empty | addresses and cidr ranges that are never scored | with the defaults, two exploit-path requests inside ten minutes are enough. ten anonymous requests for paths that do not exist are also enough. a scanner reaches either in seconds; a person browsing your library reaches neither. the allowlist takes a comma separated list of addresses and ranges, for example . use it for an office or a vpn exit you connect from, not for your lan, which is already exempt. seeing and lifting bans settings > security lists every active ban with the address, why it was banned, the last path it asked for, how many offences it racked up, and when the ban lifts. every ban has an undo button next to it. you can also ban an address by hand from the same screen. the server refuses to ban anything on your own network, so a slip of the keyboard cannot cut you off from your own dashboard. ::callout if you ever lock yourself out, the ban only affects the network path it came in on. reach the server on its lan address and the dashboard opens normally, because addresses on your own network are never banned. :: feeding the list to pfsense when the server is reached through a cloudflare tunnel, cloudflare is already blocking most of this traffic before it ever reaches your machine. when you use the regular port forwarding option instead, there is nothing in front of the server, so your firewall is the only place a bad address can be stopped before it costs you bandwidth. the server publishes its active bans as a plain text list, one address per line, at a url that only you know. pfblockerng on pfsense can pull that url on a schedule. you do not need ssh, an api key or any credential of ours on the firewall. it is one url, pasted once. copy the url from settings > security, then in pfsense: 1. go to firewall > pfblockerng > ipv4 and press add. 2. give the alias a name, for example , and set list action to . 3. under ipv4 source definitions, paste the url, set format to and state to . 4. set update frequency to . 5. save, then go to update, choose force > reload, and run it. pfblockerng will now pick up new bans on its own schedule and drop expired ones when they leave the list. if the url ever leaks, press rotate on the same settings screen. the old url stops working immediately, so update it in pfblockerng afterwards. ::callout the list contains addresses that attacked you, which is information worth keeping private. that is why the url carries a secret token. treat it like a password and do not post it anywhere public. :: related - networking - port forwarding and tunnel setup - configuration - startup flags and the web ui

title: What is nomercy-music-player
description: A headless, plugin-driven audio engine with crossfade, a swappable audio backend, synced lyrics, and a Web Audio equalizer, built on nomercy-player-core.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/index.ts, src/types.ts / what is nomercy-music-player is a headless audio engine: gapless queue playback, crossfade between tracks, a swappable audio backend a plain element or a full web audio graph, synced lyrics, and a plugin system, all driven by events and methods you call yourself. it ships no player chrome, no play button, no scrubber, no volume slider baked into the bundle, only the audio transport and a typed surface to drive it. everything visible on screen is code you write, or a plugin you add. it is built on , the shared kit under the whole player trio. the kit supplies the lifecycle, queue, plugin runtime, i18n, and auth; adds the one piece the kit cannot: an audio backend and every method specific to listening instead of watching, crossfade between queue items and lyrics. who it's for reach for when you're building a listening experience: a streaming app, a podcast or radio client, a music dashboard embedded inside a bigger product, and you want the ui to be genuinely yours instead of skinning someone else's chrome with css overrides. if you're composing a third kind of player entirely, not video, not music, start one level down at /nomercy-player-core instead. why it exists listening has one job that's genuinely hard: moving from one track to the next without a gap or a click, and doing it with a real overlap when the app wants a crossfade instead of a hard cut. owns that job through a swappable audio backend. the default drives a plain ; title: Recipe: Crossfade & Gapless Playback
description: Choosing between an overlapping crossfade and a true hard-cut gapless boundary, switching modes at runtime, and firing a manual crossfadeTo() independent of either.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/index.ts, packages/nomercy-player-core/src/adapters/preload/default.ts / recipe: crossfade & gapless playback crossfade covers and the config fields that shape the fade. this recipe is the task on top of it: picking the right automatic boundary behavior for your catalogue, and switching it at runtime instead of only at . two boundary strategies, one interface the automatic transition between queue items, the behavior that fires with no method call at all when a track ends, is owned by an from . two ship in the kit: | strategy | behavior | default for | |---|---|---| | | overlapping fade, before the outgoing track ends through into the incoming one. | music | | | hard cut at the natural end, no overlap. the incoming item is already warm from preloading, so the cut has no buffering pause either. | video | both are medium-neutral, nothing about is video-specific, it's simply not the music default. reach for it when your catalogue is a continuous mix, a live recording, or a gapless album where the tracks are mastered to touch exactly, cases where an audible overlap would sound wrong rather than smooth. is worth setting alongside even though the strategy itself already reports , it also gates the automatic transition path other plugins may be listening for, so the / / events never fire for a catalogue that never crossfades. switching modes at runtime swaps the active strategy on a live player, useful for a per-playlist or per-genre setting instead of a fixed -time choice: the swap cancels any transition already in flight, emitting with reason , and the new strategy takes effect from the next boundary the preload pipeline evaluates. manual crossfadeto either way is independent of whichever automatic strategy is active, it's a direct call, not something the transition strategy gates. a gapless-configured player can still fade into a specific track on a user action a "blend into this" button, a title: Plugin: Scrobble
description: ScrobblePlugin: threshold-based listen reporting (Last.fm 50%-or-4-minute rule by default) to any IScrobbler backend, no-op until you wire one in.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/plugins/scrobble/index.ts, src/plugins/scrobble/iscrobbler.ts / plugin: scrobble id tracks listened time per track against the player's own , , and events, and reports it to a configured backend: once per item on cursor change, once the accumulated listened time crosses a threshold. ships with a no-op scrobbler by default, so the plugin is inert, tracked but never reported, until a real backend is wired in. see recipe: scrobbling for implementing one. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | | the reporting backend. | | | | | fraction of the track's duration counted as "listened enough" — last.fm's 50% rule. | | | | | absolute listened-seconds ceiling. whichever of this or is reached first wins — last.fm's 4-minute rule. | | | | | tracks shorter than this are never scrobbled. | events namespaced onto the player's own bus as : | event | payload | fires when | |---|---|---| | | | right after resolves, once per item. | | | | right after resolves, once per item, the first time the threshold is crossed. | the iscrobbler port is optional, a backend with no "currently listening" concept can omit it. , the shipped default, implements both as immediately-resolving no-ops. how listened time is tracked a normal playback tick advances the event by well under a second; anything ≥2 seconds between ticks is treated as a seek or a track change and doesn't count toward listened time. this means scrubbing back and forth through a track doesn't inflate the listened total the way naively summing every delta would. methods exposes the tracked state read-only, for a ui that wants to show elapsed listened time or badge a track as scrobbled without waiting on the plugin's own events: | method | signature | notes | |---|---|---| | | | seconds of listened time accumulated for the current item so far, the same running total is checked against once it crosses the threshold. | | | | whether the current item already crossed the scrobble threshold. latches for the rest of that item's playback. | rules & restrictions - a failed or call never interrupts playback, the plugin catches the rejection and reports it through its own error channel , instead of throwing. - once a track is scrobbled, it's scrobbled, latches for the rest of that item's playback, a second threshold crossing replaying the same track without advancing doesn't scrobble again. - tracking resets fully on every change, including a scrobble mid-track from a manual , there's no cross-track carryover of listened time. how to extend it implement against a real service and pass it as : see recipe: scrobbling for a full implementation built on the / read surface above. next steps - plugin: auto-advance: the other queue-driving plugin, deciding what plays next rather than reporting what already played.

title: Native quickstart
description: One dependency and one view, on Android, the desktop, iOS and tvOS.
content: the native music player is the same library as the web one, ported rather than reimplemented: the same method names, the same events, the same error codes, all generated from one contract and checked against it on every build. what differs is the toolkit underneath. android and the desktop draw in compose, apple draws in swiftui, and both mount the same engine. android and desktop one coordinate for the engine, one for the chrome. an application that already draws its own controls takes the first and leaves the second. then the two surfaces a music app needs. is the bar that sits at the edge of every screen; is what it expands into. both read one and send one set of commands, so the two can never disagree about what is playing. ios and tvos add the swift package and take the drop-in product. the swiftui half mirrors the compose one name for name: and over the same state, with and as the pieces underneath. apple gets swiftui rather than compose because an application already drawing its chrome in swiftui does not want a second toolkit in the process. writing a plugin scrobbling, lyrics and auto-advance are plugins rather than player features, and so is whatever you need that this list does not have. the scaffold is a working plugin to copy: :::snippetfile="plugin-authoring" ::: next the methods reference lists every call the music surface answers for, and the migration guide covers moving an app off its own embedded player.

title: Migrating an app to the native player
description: Moving a Kotlin or Swift app off its own embedded audio player.
content: most apps arrive here with an audio player already in them: a media3 session wired into a service, or an avaudioplayer with a hand-drawn bar. the move is not a rewrite. the engine you have keeps decoding; what changes is who owns the queue, the crossfade and the state the bar reads. what to delete anything tracking whether playback is running, anything holding the queue and its cursor, anything deciding what plays next under shuffle or repeat, and anything converting a position into a scrubber fraction. those four are where two clients of one server drift apart, and the library holds one answer for each. keep your engine setup, your data source, your auth headers and your media session. kotlin wrap the engine you already build. where your screen read the engine directly, read or collect . where it advanced the queue itself, call and let the announcement reach the bar, the full screen and the notification at once. swap the chrome last. gives you the state and the commands the shipped surfaces take, and a screen can mount beside its own while you move one control at a time. swift the swiftui surfaces take the same state object the compose ones do, bridged through the framework. an app conforms what it has and gets and over it. what you gain by moving plugins, and one queue. scrobbling stops being a hook inside your playback code and becomes something that registers and unregisters cleanly; lyrics stop being a screen that polls the engine and become something that listens. and a queue that lives in the player rather than in a screen is a queue the lock screen, the car and a cast target can all read the same way.

title: What is nomercy-player-core
description: The shared kit nomercy-video-player and nomercy-music-player are built on: lifecycle, plugins, queue, adapters, i18n, and auth, ready to compose into your own player.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/index.ts / what is nomercy-player-core is not a player. it is the kit both nomercy players are built from: the lifecycle machine, the plugin runtime, the queue, the event bus, i18n, auth, and every swappable adapter port a media player needs before it can play a single frame. and each add one thing on top: a media backend and a handful of domain-typed methods for their own medium. everything else, they get from here. this page is written for the level below "how do i play a video." if you are building a nomercy video or music player for end users, you want /nomercy-video-player or /nomercy-music-player instead, both of which already do this work for you. this page, and the rest of this collection, is for someone building a third player library on the kit, or extending one of ours deeply enough to need to know what's actually underneath. who it's for composing a player from makes sense when you're building a headless media player for a format the trio doesn't cover a podcast player, a live radio player, a custom streaming protocol and want the lifecycle, queue, plugin, and auth machinery already solved and already tested, instead of writing it a third time. it's the same reason and don't duplicate that machinery between each other: one implementation, shared by every consumer, fixed once for all of them when a bug turns up. why it exists video and music playback share almost everything except the last mile: how a frame gets decoded and how a ui reacts to it. queueing up the next track, tracking playback phase, running plugins, resolving auth headers, switching languages, all of it is identical whether the media is a movie or a song. before this kit existed, that logic lived twice, in two libraries that could quietly drift apart. now it lives once, and and compose it onto their own prototypes instead of reimplementing it. a fix or a new capability that lands here reaches both libraries in the same release. the setup, then freedom, model the kit borrows a shape you may recognize from other web player setups: is strict, everything after it is yours. call once and the kit walks a fixed, non-negotiable pipeline: it snapshots your config, wires cross-cutting policies visibility, network, wake-lock, metrics, then runs through → → → → before settling the promise. call twice, or call it after , and it throws instead of leaving your instance in an ambiguous half-configured state. there is exactly one way in. what happens on top of that is not prescribed at all. the kit ships no ui, no dom beyond a container element, and no opinion about what your button looks like. every non-lifecycle behavior, from the media backend to the storage layer to how subtitles get parsed, is a named interface with a default implementation you can override wholesale: , , , , , , , , , . plugins extend behavior without forking core at all, through a base class and a cancellable event pipeline that lets a plugin veto, delay, or rewrite a mutation before it lands. what you get - lifecycle: / / and a phase machine → → → / → that every mixin and plugin can trust. - shared playback primitives: transport, time, volume, queue, and backlog methods, composed once and reused by both real players instead of hand-copied. - plugin runtime: a base class, typed registration, and a cancellable dispatch pipeline , for behavior that shouldn't require forking the player. - adapter ports: swappable interfaces for the media backend, stream source, storage, event bus, cue parsing, translation, platform capabilities wake lock, network, visibility, fullscreen, pip, realtime channel, preload strategy, transition strategy, and shuffle strategy, each with a working default. - auth-aware fetch: one pipeline 401 refresh-and-retry, 403 propagates, never conflated used by every kit-internal request and available to plugins via . - i18n engine: a translator with the kit's own strings built in english eager, every other kit locale loaded lazily on demand, consumer async-loadable bundles, and a title-token interpolation system for per-library tokens like season/episode. - cue parsing: built-in vtt, sprite-vtt, and lrc parsers behind a registry you can add your own formats to. - typed errors: a hierarchy , , , , , , ... with severity, scope, and a retry policy, instead of raw thrown strings. - composition primitives: , , and , the exact three functions and use to become players. quickstart shows them composing a real, minimal one. where it sits both rows at layer 2 sit on the same foundation and never talk to each other. and don't share code because one imports the other; they share it because both are composed from this kit. next steps - quickstart: compose a minimal title: Player and Plugin
description: The this-versus-this.player boundary that organises the whole trio: what you extend is this, what you talk to is this.player, and that line decides whether a behaviour is a player concern or a plugin concern.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/core/plugin/base.ts, src/core/state.ts, packages/nomercy-video-player/src/index.ts / core: player and plugin there is one rule underneath everything else in this trio, and once it is named the rest of the library stops feeling like a pile of methods and starts feeling like one shape. the rule is about what means. what you extend is . what you talk to is . a plugin subclasses , so inside a plugin is the plugin. its own machinery is bare : , , , , , , , , . every one of those is scoped to the plugin and cleaned up when the plugin goes away. the player is not part of the plugin. it is a collaborator the plugin holds a reference to, and you reach it through : the player is built the same way, one layer down. is not written as a class full of methods. it is composed: stamps the shared core mixins transport, time, volume, queue onto its prototype, and the per-library file adds the handful of methods its medium needs. inside any of those mixin bodies, is the player. , , are the player's own methods calling each other. there is no in there, because in there already is the player. so the boundary is symmetric. from a plugin, the player is the collaborator: . from inside the player, a plugin is the collaborator, reached the mirror way, through : for the thing you are, for the thing you are talking to. that is the entire rule. the rule is also a decision because marks what a piece of code is part of, the same boundary answers the question every new feature runs into: where does this behaviour live? if a behaviour is part of what the player is, it belongs on the player: a core mixin when it is identical for video and music, a per-library method when it carries a domain twist. you call it from inside, consumers call it from outside, and every plugin gets it for free through . if a behaviour is something layered onto a player from outside, it belongs in a plugin: , its state and lifecycle scoped to , the player reached through . autohide is the worked example. controls fading out after a few idle seconds sounds like a ui detail, so it is tempting to build it inside whatever plugin draws the controls. but "am i being interacted with right now" is a fact about the player, true whether or not any particular ui is mounted, and every ui wants the same answer. so activity tracking is a player concern: the player watches its own container, keeps / on its element, and emits . a ui plugin does not compute it. it reads 's classes, or subscribes to the event. ask "is this part of the thing, or a consumer of the thing," and the boundary tells you which side to build on. why this is the shape of the trio the same boundary, read at each layer, is why the three packages fit together the way they do. and do not share code by importing each other. they share it because both are composed onto their own prototype. the core mixins are for both players at once, which is exactly why a fix there reaches both in one release, and exactly why the core rules say a method that would branch on "is this music or video" does not belong in core: a branch means the behaviour is not really shared, so it is not really part of the thing both players are. and plugins ride on top of all of it without forking any of it, because a plugin only ever talks to 's public surface. it never reaches inside the composition. that is what lets the same /nomercy-player-core/tour/plugin-base base work against a video player, a music player, or a third library you compose yourself: the plugin does not know or care which player it is talking to, only that exposes the shared contract. next steps - the plugin base: every helper on the side, and how registration wires a plugin to its player. - adapters & dependency injection: the third kind of collaborator, the swappable ports a player is built from.

plays, and feeding it back in so the next session resumes where the last one left off. saving progress as it plays fires , throttled by 5 seconds by default, cheap enough to persist on every fire without debouncing again in your own code: fires far more often every native , dozens of times a second and is the wrong signal for a persistence write, it exists for scrubber ui, not for storage. always save from . the watchprogress shape attach the saved record to the matching field on the item the next time you build a playlist, this is the exact shape expects: what setup does with it, and what autoplay gates every call with a non-empty playlist picks a start item from on its own, no extra config needed, and does it whether or not is set: the most recently watched item wins, over 90% watched rolls forward to the next item instead of replaying the credits, anything else resumes at . rides the load down to the backend, so the stream begins fetching at the offset directly, no play-then-immediately-seek flash. is the one thing this selection doesn't do by itself: it decides whether that primed item also starts playing, or the player mounts paused and ready on the right item and position instead. this means the feed-in half of the recipe is just: know the last-watched item and its before you call . everything else, picking which item, deciding whether to resume or roll the call site. override one group in a subclass the default binding set is built from small group methods , , , and so on, each one focused on a single concern. override one to change just that group and inherit everything else unchanged: this is the same technique /nomercy-video-player/plugins-adapters/tv-key-handler itself uses: it subclasses the desktop and overrides only , , , and , every title: Plugin: Subtitle Overlay
description: SubtitleOverlayPlugin: renders the subtitleCue event stream as a positioned, WebVTT-layout-accurate DOM overlay, pooled per active cue, styled from subtitleStyle().
content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player/src/plugins/subtitle-overlay/index.ts / plugin: subtitle overlay id is the vtt rendering half of subtitle support, it turns the player's event stream sidecar vtt parsed by the kit, or native cuechange forwarded by the backend into a styled, positioned dom tree above the video. it is a pure consumer: every "where do cues come from" concern lives upstream, in the kit and the video backend, this plugin only paints what it's handed. options currently has no configurable fields, add the plugin as-is: visual customization goes through see subtitles & text tracks, not plugin options, the plugin repaints every active cue immediately on the event. dom tree and cue pooling / pairs are pooled, one per currently-active cue, so two cues active at different positions at once render as two independently-positioned boxes, matching how a browser's native vtt renderer handles simultaneous cues. when cues at overlapping positions would collide, later cues are nudged along the line axis, mirroring the webvtt cue-layout collision-avoidance step instead of letting two lines paint on top of each other. the overlay itself is sized and positioned to the actual video display rectangle , letterbox-fit under , not the container, so subtitles never sit inside letterbox padding on a wide container playing a narrower-aspect video. cue geometry cue / / / map to css following the webvtt 1.0 cue-layout algorithm: horizontal / derive from , , and an alignment anchor 0 / 0.5 / 1 for start/center/end; vertical anchor picks or based on which half of the safezone falls in, approximating the native renderer's overflow fallback. the safezone itself uses a 5% top/bottom, 3% left/right inset, calibrated for widescreen delivery rather than the crt-era 5%/5% smpte convention, matching what modern streamers ship. rules & restrictions - renders only, it never touches subtitle selection, that's kit surface , . selecting a track with this plugin not loaded changes state correctly and paints nothing, see subtitles & text tracks. - ass/ssa tracks are not this plugin's job, /nomercy-video-player/plugins-adapters/octopus renders those; both plugins coexist safely because they react to different signals native cue events here, the selection event there and each tears its own rendering down for formats it doesn't own. - colors resolve through a 2d-canvas-normalized hex conversion with an alpha byte folded in from / / , so any css color string in named color, , hex works, not just hex literals. how to extend it there's no subclass hook, the plugin is a leaf consumer of and . a genuinely different rendering strategy canvas-based, webgl, a different cue-collision algorithm is a new plugin against the same two signals rather than a subclass of this one: don't register both and a custom renderer for the same format at once, both would paint the same cue stream independently and double up the dom. next steps - plugin: octopus ass/ssa subtitles: the renderer for the format this plugin intentionally leaves alone.

mobile additionally splits two rows off the top and bottom of the center column for volume up/down, detected via presence or . | zone | single-tap | double-tap | |---|---|---| | left seek back | dismiss controls if visible, no-op otherwise, already woke them. | seek back . | | center playback | toggle playback unless . | toggle fullscreen. | | right seek forward | dismiss controls if visible, no-op otherwise, already woke them. | seek forward . | | top / bottom of center, mobile only | dismiss controls if visible, no-op otherwise, already woke them. | volume up / down. | each seek zone shows a floating circular indicator chevron icon plus accumulated seconds, e.g. "-30s" after three rapid taps that lazily mounts on first use and collapses back to zero after roughly a second of no further taps in that direction. rules & restrictions - single-tap "toggle controls" reads a snapshot of visibility captured at in the capture phase, before 's own bubble-phase wake handler can mutate the dom. without this, a tap from a hidden state would show controls on and then immediately hide them again when the deferred single-tap handler read the just-added class, a show-then-hide flicker that makes the tap look like it did nothing. - mobile detection is a one-shot capability check at plugin startup presence or , not a live pointer-type check, a touch-capable laptop used with a mouse still gets the mobile volume zones. - emits to coordinate with 's auto-hide timer, this plugin has no visible chrome of its own to hide. how to extend it there's no subclass hook for zone geometry, the grid positions are internal. a different zone layout a 5-zone grid, a corner-only seek gesture is a new plugin built against the same player methods , , , , , rather than a subclass: next steps - plugin: desktop ui: the control bar this plugin's events show and hide.

title: Native quickstart
description: One dependency and one view, on Android, the desktop, iOS and tvOS.
content: the native video player is the same library as the web one, ported rather than reimplemented: the same method names, the same events, the same error codes, all generated from one contract and checked against it on every build. what differs is the toolkit underneath. android and the desktop draw in compose, apple draws in swiftui, and both mount the same engine. android and desktop one coordinate for the engine, one for the chrome. an application that already draws its own controls takes the first and leaves the second. then one view. reads the device it is on and mounts the touch chrome or the focus chrome accordingly, so the same call is a phone player and a television player with different hands on it. :::snippetfile="kotlin-quickstart" ::: the engine is on android and on the desktop. both implement the same , so everything above the seam is identical and the only per-platform line is the one that constructs the engine. ios and tvos add the swift package and take the drop-in product. draws the controls and reads everything it shows off the object you hand it. is the projection it observes, and it forwards to anything conforming to , which is seven members. :::snippetfile="swift-quickstart" ::: apple gets swiftui rather than compose because an application already drawing its chrome in swiftui does not want a second toolkit in the process. next the methods reference lists every call the video surface answers for, and the migration guide covers moving an app off its own embedded player.

title: Migrating an app to the native player
description: Moving a Kotlin or Swift app off its own embedded player.
content: most apps arrive here with a player already in them: an exoplayer wired directly into a screen, or an avplayer with hand-drawn controls. the move is not a rewrite. the engine you have keeps decoding; what changes is who owns the state above it and who draws the controls. what to delete the parts worth removing are the ones this library already answers for, and the list is longer than it looks. anything tracking whether playback is running, anything converting a position into a progress fraction, anything remembering a selected subtitle across a track change, and anything deciding when the controls hide. those are the four places two clients of the same server drift apart, and they are the four the library holds one answer for. keep your engine setup, your data source, your auth headers and your surface. kotlin wrap the engine you already build rather than replacing it. is a , so everything the core reference lists is on it. where your screen read , read or collect . where it called , call and let the announcement reach anything else listening. swap your controls last. takes the player and an optional surface, and a screen can mount it beside its own chrome while you move one control at a time. swift conform what you have to rather than adopting a new engine. it is seven members: the , an observe callback, three transport calls and three selection calls. hand that to and the chrome works over it. the engine adapter for the kotlin core is not shipped yet. until it is, an apple app conforms its own avfoundation code to and gets the full chrome over it, which is the path the quickstart shows. what you gain by moving plugins. once the player owns the state, a feature is a plugin rather than a change to a screen: it registers, listens, contributes ui, and unregisters cleanly. the plugin scaffold is a working one to copy, and the shipped testing kit tests it without a device.
